extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history and philosophy of science; readers interested in Bacon and the development of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating the methodological principles and standards (induction, experiment, rejection of authority, utility, etc.) associated with Francis Bacon and his antecedents as presented in a historical/introduction text. The focus is on criteria for good scientific inquiry and the influence of Bacon's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of knowledge in the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientiarum omnium et geometriae ipsius principia a sensu haberi, vel proxima eorum, quae sensu percepta sunt; the origin of all knowledge lies in sensory perception (knowledge begins with the senses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge and first principles should be traced back to what is perceived by the senses; many authors (Aristotle, Telesius, Campanella, Caesalpinus) assert this. Use close observation of particulars as the basis for general claims rather than starting from abstract axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of experience and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sine experientia nihil sufficienter sciri potest ('Without experience nothing can be known sufficiently'); experimental (experientalis) science is described as the 'mater' or 'domina' of the sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise performing experiments to establish and verify scientific conclusions; use experiments to refute common errors (examples given: refuting vulgar errors like myths about diamonds). Experimental practice should accompany theoretical argument to secure truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments alone do not certify truth — verify by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Argumentum concludit sed non certificat neque removet dubitationem, ut quiescat animus in intu tu veritatis, nisi eam inveniat via experientiae; arguments may conclude but do not remove doubt unless the way of experience is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purely deductive or rhetorical argumentation as insufficient; require empirical confirmation. Be wary of conclusions based solely on authority or purely logical deduction without experimental corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction over traditional syllogistic logic
rubrics_metrics.description: The text contrasts two modes of knowing — per argumentum and per experiment — and advocates a method proceeding 'per Inductionem' in preference to the syllogistic logic that merely governs disputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor building general principles from systematic observation and induction rather than relying on syllogism to win disputes; develop a 'new logic' that tests the principles of the sciences themselves (Novum Organum idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence: observation → experiment → discover cause → formulate rule → test
rubrics_metrics.description: A methodological precept repeated (Leonardo, Venturi): begin by observation, pass to experiment, with the help of experiment seek to determine the cause, then formulate a rule and submit it to calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the procedural flow: careful observation of particulars, controlled experiment(s), inference of causal relations, formulation of general laws, and quantitative or calculational testing of those laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject reliance on authority (argument from Authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument from Authority had been combated; authors repeatedly emphasise breaking the 'yoke of authority' and consulting nature/experience rather than accepting ancient authors uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uncritical deference to ancient or prestigious authorities (Aristotle, Plato, Galen, etc.). Prefer direct engagement with nature and experiments; treat authorities as possible starting-points but not final arbiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility as an end of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilitas cujuslibet rei consideranda est — utility of any thing must be considered; both Bacons attach exaggerated importance to utility as the end of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scientific work also by its practical usefulness and potential application to the arts and human affairs; communicate prospective benefits to secure interest and support. Recognise that perceived lack of utility may limit uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary comprehension — study sciences in mutual relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The comprehensive view and the necessity of studying the various sciences in their mutual relations are emphasized as important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work for awareness of related fields and the mutual relevance of findings; consider how methods/principles apply across disciplines rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive method should be applicable across all sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Novum Organum: our method, which proceeds by Induction, comprises all sciences (induction is not limited to natural philosophy but extends to other sciences, logic, ethics, politics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging methodological claims, test whether inductive approaches are argued as generalizable and appropriately adapted to different subject-matters; prefer methods argued to have cross-disciplinary validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and avoid sources of error (the 'four causes of error' / Idola)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to four causes of error ('comprehendendae veritatis offendicula') compared with Bacon's 'Idola' — sources or idols that impede true knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work recognises typical epistemic pitfalls (idola/species of error) and includes strategies to detect or remove them. Use this as a criterion for methodological rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experiments and demonstrations over probable conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast experiments and demonstrations with probable conjectures and vulgar philosophizing; favour experimental demonstration as the core of new philosophy (Gilbert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give more weight to demonstrated experimental results and reproducible demonstrations than to speculative or merely probable hypotheses; require empirical grounding for claims presented as factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic (resolutiva) method: work from effect back to cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation of the 'methodus resolutiva' or analytic method — working backwards from the effect to the cause — in preference to the 'methodus compositiva' or synthetic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work adopts an analytic approach where appropriate (examining particulars to infer wholes/causes) and whether that approach is applied systematically and rigorously rather than casually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: experience alone is not sufficient without critical elimination of idols
rubrics_metrics.description: While Paracelsus and others appealed strongly to experience, Bacon and commentators caution that appeal to experience by itself may be insufficient ('the appeal to experience was in itself by no means sufficient to conduct them to truth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge empirical work on whether it combines observation/experiment with critical reflection and procedures designed to eliminate biases, faulty interpretations, or 'vertiginous' experiential confusions; do not treat raw experience as automatically authoritative.
